questions.question_text: Two bodies are projected with the same velocity. If one is projected at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ and the other at $45^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, then the ratio of maximum heights attained is
questions.question_html: Two bodies are projected with the same velocity. If one is projected at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ and the other at $45^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, then the ratio of maximum heights attained is
questions.explanation_text: For a projectile, the maximum height is given by $H=\frac{u^{2}sin^{2}\theta}{2g}$ Here both bodies are projected with the same velocity, so $u$ is the same for both. Also, $g$ is the same. So maximum height depends only on $sin^{2}\theta$ . For the first body, $\theta=30^{\circ}$ $H_{1}=\frac{u^{2}sin^{2}30^{\circ}}{2g}$ For the second body, $\theta=45^{\circ}$ $H_{2}=\frac{u^{2}sin^{2}45^{\circ}}{2g}$ So, $\frac{H_{1}}{H_{2}}=\frac{sin^{2}30^{\circ}}{sin^{2}45^{\circ}}$ We know, $sin30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$ and $sin45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ So, $\frac{H_{1}}{H_{2}}=\frac{(\frac{1}{2})^{2}}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}}$ $=\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$ Hence, $H_{1}:H_{2}=1:2$ The correct option is Option B, $1:2$ .
questions.explanation_html:
For a projectile, the maximum height is given by

$H=\frac{u^{2}sin^{2}\theta}{2g}$

Here both bodies are projected with the same velocity, so $u$ is the same for both. Also, $g$ is the same.

So maximum height depends only on $sin^{2}\theta$ .

For the first body,

$\theta=30^{\circ}$

$H_{1}=\frac{u^{2}sin^{2}30^{\circ}}{2g}$

For the second body,

$\theta=45^{\circ}$

$H_{2}=\frac{u^{2}sin^{2}45^{\circ}}{2g}$

So,

$\frac{H_{1}}{H_{2}}=\frac{sin^{2}30^{\circ}}{sin^{2}45^{\circ}}$

We know,

$sin30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$

and

$sin45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

So,

$\frac{H_{1}}{H_{2}}=\frac{(\frac{1}{2})^{2}}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}}$

$=\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$

Hence,

$H_{1}:H_{2}=1:2$

The correct option is Option B, $1:2$ .

questions.question_text: In the projectile motion of a particle on a level ground, which of the following remains constant with reference to time and position?
questions.question_html: In the projectile motion of a particle on a level ground, which of the following remains constant with reference to time and position?

options.label: A
options.text: Average velocity between any two points on the path
options.html: Average velocity between any two points on the path

options.label: B
options.html: Horizontal component of velocity

options.label: C
options.text: Angle between the instantaneous velocity with the horizontal
options.html: Angle between the instantaneous velocity with the horizontal

options.label: D
options.text: Vertical component of the velocity of the projectile
options.html: Vertical component of the velocity of the projectile

questions.explanation_text: The only quantity that stays unchanged (no acceleration in that direction) is the horizontal component of the velocity. In symbols: • If the launch speed is $u$ at an angle $\theta$ above horizontal, $v_{x}=ucos\theta$ and since there’s no horizontal acceleration, $v_{x}$ remains the same at all times and positions. So the correct choice is: Option B: Horizontal component of velocity.
questions.explanation_html:
The only quantity that stays unchanged (no acceleration in that direction) is the horizontal component of the velocity. In symbols:

• If the launch speed is $u$ at an angle $\theta$ above horizontal,

$v_{x}=ucos\theta$

and since there’s no horizontal acceleration, $v_{x}$ remains the same at all times and positions.

So the correct choice is:

Option B: Horizontal component of velocity.

questions.question_text: Two objects are projected at an angle $\theta^{\circ}$ and $(90-\theta^{\circ})$ , to the horizontal with the same speed. The ratio of their maximum vertical heights is
questions.question_html: Two objects are projected at an angle $\theta^{\circ}$ and $(90-\theta^{\circ})$ , to the horizontal with the same speed. The ratio of their maximum vertical heights is
questions.explanation_text: We know that, maximum vertical height in projectile motion, $H=\frac{u^{2}sin^{2}\phi}{2g}$ [where, $\phi$ is angle of projection.] $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & H∝sin^{2}\phi \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{H_{1}}{H_{2}}=\frac{sin^{2}\phi}{sin^{2}\phi_{2}}=\frac{sin^{2}\theta}{sin^{2}(90-\theta)} \end{aligned}$ [Given, $\phi_{1}=\theta$ and $\phi_{2}=90^{\circ}-\theta$ ] $=\frac{sin^{2}\theta}{cos^{2}\theta}=tan^{2}\theta$ $\therefore H_{1}:H_{2}=tan^{2}\theta:1$
questions.explanation_html:
We know that, maximum vertical height in projectile motion,

$H=\frac{u^{2}sin^{2}\phi}{2g}$ [where, $\phi$ is angle of projection.]

$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & H∝sin^{2}\phi \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{H_{1}}{H_{2}}=\frac{sin^{2}\phi}{sin^{2}\phi_{2}}=\frac{sin^{2}\theta}{sin^{2}(90-\theta)} \end{aligned}$

[Given, $\phi_{1}=\theta$ and $\phi_{2}=90^{\circ}-\theta$ ]

$=\frac{sin^{2}\theta}{cos^{2}\theta}=tan^{2}\theta$

$\therefore H_{1}:H_{2}=tan^{2}\theta:1$

questions.question_html: A particle starts from the origin at $t=0$ with a velocity of $10\hat{j}ms^{-1}$ and move in the $x$ - $y$ plane with a constant acceleration of $(8\hat{i}+2\hat{j})ms^{-2}$ . At an instant when the $x$ -coordinate of the particle is $16m,y$ -coordinate of the particle is
questions.explanation_text: Given, $u=10\hat{j}ms^{-1},a=8\hat{i}+2\hat{j}ms^{-2}$ $x=16m$ Using equation of motion, $\begin{aligned} s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2} \\ x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}=10\hat{j} \times t+\frac{1}{2}(8\hat{i}+2\hat{j})t^{2} \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow 16\hat{i}+y\hat{j}=10\hat{j}+4t^{2}\hat{i}+t^{2}\hat{j}$ Comparing both sides, we get $\begin{aligned} & 4t^{2}=16 \\ \Rightarrow & t=2s \\ \text{and} & y=10t+t^{2} \\ & =10 \times 2+(2)^{2} \\ & =24m \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, $u=10\hat{j}ms^{-1},a=8\hat{i}+2\hat{j}ms^{-2}$

$x=16m$

Using equation of motion,

$\begin{aligned} s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2} \\ x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}=10\hat{j} \times t+\frac{1}{2}(8\hat{i}+2\hat{j})t^{2} \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow 16\hat{i}+y\hat{j}=10\hat{j}+4t^{2}\hat{i}+t^{2}\hat{j}$

Comparing both sides, we get

$\begin{aligned} & 4t^{2}=16 \\ \Rightarrow & t=2s \\ \text{and} & y=10t+t^{2} \\ & =10 \times 2+(2)^{2} \\ & =24m \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: The maximum range of a gun on horizontal plane is $16km$ . If $g=10ms^{-2}$ , then muzzle velocity of a shell is
questions.question_html: The maximum range of a gun on horizontal plane is $16km$ . If $g=10ms^{-2}$ , then muzzle velocity of a shell is
questions.explanation_text: The maximum range $R$ of a projectile on a horizontal plane is given by the formula: $R=\frac{v^{2}sin2\theta}{g}$ For the maximum range, $\theta$ is $45^{\circ}$ , and $sin2\theta=sin90^{\circ}=1$ . Hence, the formula simplifies to: $R=\frac{v^{2}}{g}$ We can rearrange this equation to solve for the initial muzzle velocity $v$ : $v^{2}=R \cdot g$ $v=\sqrt{R \cdot g}$ Given: $R=16\text{km}=16000\text{m}$ $g=10\text{m/s}^{2}$ Substitute these values into the equation: $v=\sqrt{16000 \cdot 10}$ $v=\sqrt{160000}$ $v=400\text{m/s}$ Therefore, the muzzle velocity of a shell is Option C: $400\text{m/s}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
The maximum range $R$ of a projectile on a horizontal plane is given by the formula:

$R=\frac{v^{2}sin2\theta}{g}$

For the maximum range, $\theta$ is $45^{\circ}$ , and $sin2\theta=sin90^{\circ}=1$ . Hence, the formula simplifies to:

$R=\frac{v^{2}}{g}$

We can rearrange this equation to solve for the initial muzzle velocity $v$ :

$v^{2}=R \cdot g$

$v=\sqrt{R \cdot g}$

Given:

$R=16\text{km}=16000\text{m}$

$g=10\text{m/s}^{2}$

Substitute these values into the equation:

$v=\sqrt{16000 \cdot 10}$

$v=\sqrt{160000}$

$v=400\text{m/s}$

Therefore, the muzzle velocity of a shell is Option C: $400\text{m/s}$ .

questions.question_text: Rain is falling vertically with a speed of $12ms^{-1}$ . A woman rides a bicycles with a speed of $12ms^{-1}$ in east to west direction. What is the direction in which she should hold her umbrella?
questions.question_html: Rain is falling vertically with a speed of $12ms^{-1}$ . A woman rides a bicycles with a speed of $12ms^{-1}$ in east to west direction. What is the direction in which she should hold her umbrella?

options.label: A
options.html: $30^{\circ}$ , towards east

options.label: B
options.html: $45^{\circ}$ , towards east

options.label: C
options.html: $30^{\circ}$ , towards west

options.label: D
options.html: $45^{\circ}$ , towards west

questions.explanation_text: The given situation is shown below Here, velocity of rain, $v_{r}=12ms^{-1}$ and velocity of woman, $v_{w}=12ms^{-1}$ The relative velocity of rain w.r.t. woman is $\begin{aligned} v_{nw} & =\sqrt{v_{w}^{2}+v_{r}^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{(12)^{2}+(12)^{2}}=12\sqrt{2}ms^{-1} \end{aligned}$ The direction in which the woman should hold her umbrella is $\begin{aligned} sin\theta & =\frac{v_{w}}{v_{rw}}=\frac{12}{12\sqrt{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \theta & =sin^{-1}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})=45^{\circ},\text{towards east} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
The given situation is shown below

Here, velocity of rain, $v_{r}=12ms^{-1}$

and velocity of woman, $v_{w}=12ms^{-1}$

The relative velocity of rain w.r.t. woman is

$\begin{aligned} v_{nw} & =\sqrt{v_{w}^{2}+v_{r}^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{(12)^{2}+(12)^{2}}=12\sqrt{2}ms^{-1} \end{aligned}$

The direction in which the woman should hold her umbrella is

$\begin{aligned} sin\theta & =\frac{v_{w}}{v_{rw}}=\frac{12}{12\sqrt{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \theta & =sin^{-1}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})=45^{\circ},\text{towards east} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: The trajectory of a projectile projected from origin is given by the equation $y=x-\frac{2x^{2}}{5}$ . The initial velocity of the projectile is
questions.question_html: The trajectory of a projectile projected from origin is given by the equation $y=x-\frac{2x^{2}}{5}$ . The initial velocity of the projectile is
questions.explanation_text: The trajectory of a projectile launched from the origin is represented by the equation: $y=x-\frac{2x^{2}}{5}$ We'll compare this equation with the standard trajectory equation for a projectile: $y=xtan\theta-\frac{g}{2u^{2}cos^{2}\theta}x^{2}$ From this comparison, we find: $tan\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=45^{\circ}$ This indicates that the angle of projection is $45^{\circ}$ . At the range ( $R$ ), the height ( $y=0$ ) because the projectile returns to the horizontal axis: From the given equation: $0=R-\frac{2R^{2}}{5}0=R(1-\frac{2R}{5}) \Rightarrow R \ne 0 \therefore 1-\frac{2R}{5}=0 \Rightarrow R=\frac{5}{2}$ Here, $R$ is the range of the projectile. Using the range formula for projectiles: $R=\frac{u^{2}sin(2 \times 45^{\circ})}{g}$ Substitute the known values: $\frac{u^{2}}{10}=\frac{5}{2}[g=10\text{m/s}^{2}]u^{2}=\frac{5}{2} \times 10 \Rightarrow u=5\text{m/s}$ Therefore, the initial velocity $u$ of the projectile is $5\text{m/s}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
The trajectory of a projectile launched from the origin is represented by the equation:

$y=x-\frac{2x^{2}}{5}$

We'll compare this equation with the standard trajectory equation for a projectile:

$y=xtan\theta-\frac{g}{2u^{2}cos^{2}\theta}x^{2}$

From this comparison, we find:

$tan\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=45^{\circ}$

This indicates that the angle of projection is $45^{\circ}$ .

At the range ( $R$ ), the height ( $y=0$ ) because the projectile returns to the horizontal axis:

From the given equation:

$0=R-\frac{2R^{2}}{5}0=R(1-\frac{2R}{5}) \Rightarrow R \ne 0 \therefore 1-\frac{2R}{5}=0 \Rightarrow R=\frac{5}{2}$

Here, $R$ is the range of the projectile.

Using the range formula for projectiles:

$R=\frac{u^{2}sin(2 \times 45^{\circ})}{g}$

Substitute the known values:

$\frac{u^{2}}{10}=\frac{5}{2}[g=10\text{m/s}^{2}]u^{2}=\frac{5}{2} \times 10 \Rightarrow u=5\text{m/s}$

Therefore, the initial velocity $u$ of the projectile is $5\text{m/s}$ .
